outlooks.summary: Scattered severe thunderstorms should occur today and tonight mainly from parts of Iowa into southern Minnesota/Wisconsin and northern Illinois. Large to very large hail, significant severe winds, and a few tornadoes all appear possible.

sections.title: Upper Midwest
sections.text: A large-scale upper trough/low is forecast to move eastward today from the Canadian Prairie provinces and the northern Plains over Ontario and the Upper Midwest. Farther west, and upper high will remain centered over the Four Corners region. An EML emanating from the higher terrain of the Southwest and southern/central Rockies will overspread much of the Upper Midwest. The cap associated with this EML should tend to suppress robust convection through much of the day. At the surface, a cold front should move southeastward across MN and northern WI through the day. This front should be located across central/southern WI into southern MN and northern IA by peak afternoon heating, and it will likely serve as a focus for severe storm development. A narrow corridor of rich low-level moisture characterized by upper 60s to low 70s surface dewpoints should be present ahead of the cold front. Strong heating is expected across the warm sector, and the presence of steep mid-level lapse rates will likely contribute to very strong instability (MLCAPE 3500-5000+ J/kg) from far eastern NE into northern IA, southern MN, and southwestern WI. outlooks.summary: Severe storms are expected late this afternoon into tonight for parts of the upper Mississippi Valley, from northern Iowa/southern Minnesota into southern Wisconsin and northern Illinois. Wind gusts near or exceeding 75 mph, hail up to the size of baseballs, and a couple of tornadoes will be possible.

sections.title: Upper MS Valley this afternoon into tonight
sections.text: A midlevel shortwave trough over the northern Plains/southern Prairie Provinces has crested the ridge, and heights will be suppressed east-southeastward toward the upper MS Valley and upper Great lakes by tonight. An associated, weak surface cold front/trough will likewise move slowly southeastward across NE/IA/MN/WI through tonight. The front and any lingering outflow boundaries from overnight convection will likely focus afternoon and evening thunderstorm development across southeast MN and along the IA/MN border, in phase with an embedded speed max moving eastward from SD (as evidence by the weak midlevel convection over SD this morning). The thermodynamic environment will feature steep midlevel lapse rates with a warm elevated mixed layer extending eastward from the Rockies, atop boundary-layer dewpoints in the 65-70 F range. Strong surface heating in the wake of morning elevated convection will drive large buoyancy (MLCAPE in excess of 4000 J/kg) and weakening convective inhibition as surface temperatures warm into the 90s. sections.title: AR this afternoon/evening
sections.text: A remnant MCV over west central MO this morning will continue southward over AR by later this afternoon. Strong surface heating (temperatures warming into the lower 90s) and boundary-layer dewpoints in the lower 70s will support MLCAPE in excess of 3000 J/kg, and isolated to widely scattered thunderstorms are expected to form by mid-late afternoon. Deep-layer, north-northeasterly shear of 20-30 kt and DCAPE in excess of 1200 J/kg suggest that any cells/small clusters will move toward the south-southwest with the potential to produce isolated damaging downbursts and large hail for a few hours this late afternoon/evening. ..Thompson/Leitman.. 06/17/2021

outlooks.summary: Severe storms are expected late this afternoon into tonight across parts of the Upper Mississippi Valley, from central/southern Wisconsin and southern Minnesota into northern portions of Iowa and Illinois. A few tornadoes, damaging wind gusts exceeding 75 mph, and hail up to the size of baseballs will be possible.

sections.title: Upper MS Valley
sections.text: Primary change from prior outlook is to expand greater probabilities farther north/east across parts of WI and IL, with the expectation of the wind threat persisting longer in this region tonight. A mid-level impulse/speed max over SD, responsible for morning ACCAS across the eastern portion of the state, will aid in ascent along a southeast-moving cold front. Thunderstorm initiation is expected across west-central WI into southeast MN as MLCIN wanes near the front during the late afternoon. Activity should eventually backbuild southwestward into northeast/north-central IA this evening, but uncertainty is greater with how far into central IA convection will ultimately become sustained owing to greater influence of the EML and persistence of a relatively hot/dry boundary-layer across KS/southern NE into southern IA. sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: The only changes this forecast update are the following: 1) Added a 5-percent wind probability over parts of the central High Plains for late afternoon/early evening for the risk of isolated microbursts. Extremely steep lapse rates from the surface up to 450 mb will favor evaporation potential with any locally stronger cores that can develop. Slightly stronger mid- to high-level flow over northeast CO compared to areas farther south will aid in some eastward storm motion. 2) Lowered severe probabilities on the western edge of the previously issued SLGT and ENH risk areas over northern IA to reflect model guidance showing a lower probability for storm development over this region. 3) Minor adjustment to the northern part of the MRGL Risk over the Ozarks based on mid afternoon satellite trends. Elsewhere, the forecast remains on track and no other changes were made. ..Smith.. 06/17/2021 .PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1130 AM CDT Thu Jun 17 2021/

sections.title: Upper Mississippi Valley
sections.text: Severe thunderstorms with a history of significant severe hail and damaging gusts have developed since 23z, and latest mesoanalysis indicates moderate MLCAPE remains in place, along with 45-55 kts of effective shear. Low-level warm advection should increase across the SLGT/ENH portion of the risk area as a low-level jet strengthens overnight. A subtle impulse embedded within westerly mid-level flow will also contribute to ascent. Ongoing severe storms will continue to pose a damaging wind and large hail risk this evening and overnight, with significant severe hail remaining possible given supercell storm structures and steep mid-level lapse rates. Increasing storm coverage and eventual evolution into a bowing complex later this evening/overnight is anticipated, with a risk for significant severe wind gusts. A tornado or two will also remain possible with both supercell and bowing QLCS structures. ..Bunting.. 06/18/2021

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Thunderstorms are expected to increase in coverage from southern Missouri through northern and western Arkansas this afternoon. The stronger storms will become capable of producing a few instances of strong to severe wind gusts and marginally severe hail.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: As of late morning the atmosphere continues to destabilize across western through northern AR into southern MO supported by strong diabatic warming of the moist boundary layer. Temperatures rising through the upper 80s F along with low 70s dewpoints are promoting 2500-3000 J/kg MLCAPE. A weak surface boundary was also indicated from southeast OK through western and northern AR into southeast MO where boundary layer cumulus is increasing, and an isolated storm has already developed over southeast MO. As surface temperatures approach 90F, very little convective inhibition should remain and storms are expected to increase in coverage during the afternoon. An MCV was also indicated across southwest MO moving generally south, and this feature might have some influence on storm coverage. Storms will move generally southwesterly under the influence of modest north northeasterly winds aloft. Multicells / pulse storms should be the dominant modes with some activity possibly evolving into small clusters. This environment should support a few instances of hail and locally strong to damaging gusts during the afternoon.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated thunderstorm development is underway, and a gradual increase in coverage and intensity is expected through the afternoon into early evening. Large hail and damaging winds are the primary threats. Timing of the more substantial severe threat is uncertain, with current storm trends being monitored for the need of a WW issuance.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest visible satellite and MRMS mosaic radar data show isolated thunderstorm development ongoing across northern IA, southern MN, and far western WI. Modified 18Z RAP forecast soundings in proximity to the region of convective initiation show a near-saturation zone close to 700 mb, where the developing storms are likely rooted. As such, these elevated storms are expected to progress eastward over the next couple of hours in an 8+ C/km deep-layer lapse rate environment, contributing to 2000 J/kg MUCAPE above the convective inhibition layer. Though large-scale ridging is in place, embedded 700 mb perturbations cresting the ridge are likely contributing to enough deep-layer ascent for convective initiation and possibly sustenance. While diurnal mixing has reached up to 700 mb, low-level lee-troughing has resulted in the preservation of 25+ kt 850 mb southwesterly flow, overspread by 40-60 kts of westerly 500 mb winds pivoting around the upper ridge. As such, up to 50 kts of effective bulk shear is overlapping the 2000 J/kg MUCAPE environment based on 19Z mesoanalysis, with multicells and supercell structures likely the dominant convective mode initially. Large hail and damaging gusts will be the main threats, with 2+ inch diameter stones and a few 65+ kt wind gusts possible with the stronger, more organized supercells given the very steep deep-layer lapse rates. A brief tornado or two is possible before storms become more outflow dominant given relatively weak low-level shear and evaporative cooling within a dry sub-cloud layer leading to outflow dominant storm modes. With time, cold pool mergers should contribute to MCS development, with damaging winds becoming the primary threat. mesoscale_discussions.summary: The threat for severe thunderstorms continues across much of the Upper MS Valley. Large hail is the primary threat, with some damaging wind gusts possible as well. Parts of south-central/southeast MN are being monitored for additional watch issuance.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Recent surface analysis places the cold front from about 10 miles east-southeast of EAU southwestward through south-central MN and far northwest IA. A corridor of slightly higher dewpoints exists along this frontal boundary, with mid 60s dewpoints extending into far west-central WI. A few storms have developed along this front in far west-central WI, where surface temperatures were a few degrees higher, which resulted in less convective inhibition. Environment near these storms supports strong updrafts and the potential for quick upscale growth on storm outflow. Severe threat with these storms will likely persist into more of central WI. Farther west (across southwest MN), a few storms have recently developed, likely as a result of persistent warm air advection across the region. Character of the reflectivity also suggests thee storms are elevated. Steep mid-level lapse rates and resulting strong buoyancy could result in a few updrafts capable of producing large hail. Some additional development appears possible across this area with new echos now beginning to appear. Overall storm coverage remains uncertain given the warm low to mid-level temperatures and resulting convective inhibition. However, persistent isentropic ascent coupled with the approach of a subtle vorticity maximum and southward pushing 850mb front suggest potential for additional storms.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Threat for large hail and damaging wind gusts is expected to extend past the 03Z expiration of Severe Thunderstorm Watch 276.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Cluster of supercells which initiated just south of MPX has continued southeastward through southeast MN. Numerous reports of 2"+ hail have accompanied these supercells thus far. Strengthening southwesterly low-level flow will continue to provide moist inflow to this storms, helping to maintain their strengthen in spite of low-level stabilization. Some potential exists for these storms to become more outflow dominant, growing upscale into a forward-propagating MCS with damaging wind gusts as the primary severe risk. However, trends do not indicate this transition is imminent, so large hail will likely remain the primary severe risk with these storms for at least the next hour. Severe Thunderstorm Watch 276 is set to expire at 03Z. The ongoing cluster is expected to last for at least the next few hours, and likely longer if the anticipated upscale growth occurs. As such, a new watch will likely be need across portions of the region to address the ongoing severe risk. Additional development also appears possible back farther west along near the central MN/IA border. Steep lapse rates and moderate vertical shear support strong updrafts in this region if convective inhibition can be overcome.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The threat for large to very large hail and damaging wind gusts continues.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Cluster of supercells in far southeast MN has continued to produce large to very large (i.e. greater than 2" diameter) as it moves southeastward along the the MN/WI border. Recent MESH is estimating 3 to 3.5"in the storm moving across southwest Winona County, which is currently the westernmost cell in the cluster. Given its location, ample moist low-level inflow will be available to this storm and it will likely maintain a very strong updraft as it moves into LSE. Additionally, recent radar trends have begun to indicate a more southeastward motion of the entire cluster, suggesting the upscale growth/linear transition is likely underway. ..Mosier.. 06/18/2021 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A threat for large hail and isolated wind damage will likely continue for a few more hours. The threat will probably be greatest across south-central Wisconsin where a cluster of strong thunderstorms is ongoing. The storms are expected to decrease in intensity as they move eastward toward Lake Michigan where instability is weaker.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The latest surface analysis shows a 1004 mb low over far northeast Iowa with a quasi-stationary front extending eastward across south-central Wisconsin. An east-to-west line of strong to severe thunderstorms is ongoing near the front. The RAP is showing moderate instability across south-central Wisconsin with generally weaker instability with eastward extent. MUCAPE is estimated near 2500 J/Kg in southwest Wisconsin and near 1000 J/kg in southeast Wisconsin. Effective shear is estimated near 50 kt across much of south-central Wisconsin which will likely support a severe threat for a few more hours. The instability, shear and steep mid-level lapse rates evident on forecast soundings, will be favorable for large hail with the stronger updrafts. Concerning the wind-damage potential, the RAP is showing CIN values in south-central Wisconsin in the -200 to -300 J/kg range. This will make it difficult for the stronger storms to produce wind damage. Any wind-damage potential should remain relatively isolated. ..Broyles.. 06/18/2021 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...
